extracted.intended_audience: lawyers, judges, scholars, and practitioners handling military pay and disability claims (Tucker Act, correction boards, APA litigation)
extracted.subtask_short: suits for military pay and disability benefits
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of legal standards, procedural rules, and remedial practices governing litigation (and administrative exhaustion) of military pay and disability claims in courts and correction boards. Focuses on accrual/statute-of-limitations rules, standards of review, money-mandating analysis, exhaustion, disability evaluation procedures, and class-action handling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statute of limitations and accrual rules for APA-based claims
rubrics_metrics.description: In district courts, the six-year statute of limitations in 28 U.S.C. § 2401(a) applies to APA-based claims, but the accrual date depends on whether the claim relates to an underlying cause or a board determination: the underlying cause accrues at the time of the harm, while claims based on board action may not accrue until final disposition by the board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that a discharged plaintiff might wait the maximum time to file with a board (up to fifteen years) and then the maximum time to sue in district court on the board’s decision (six years), producing actions decades after the discharge (Walters v. Secretary of Defense example). Cases cited: Martinez, Smith v. Marsh, Geyen, Dougherty, Bittner, Walters. Advises practitioners to consider whether claim is board-derived or underlying when calculating accrual and timeliness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial evidence / arbitrary and capricious standard for board-derived claims
rubrics_metrics.description: When a military pay claim has been before a correctional board, judicial review is 'limited to determining whether [the] decision ... is arbitrary, capricious, unsupported by substantial evidence, or contrary to applicable statutes and regulations.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts do not reweigh evidence but determine whether the board’s conclusion is supported by substantial evidence; the court may not substitute its judgment for that of the military where reasonable minds could differ. Citation: Melendez Camilo (quoting Heisig). This standard frames briefing and the scope of evidence courts will consider.

rubrics_metrics.name: Available remedies in judicial review of military pay/benefit claims
rubrics_metrics.description: When appropriate, courts may accompany an award of monetary relief with orders 'directing restoration to office or position, placement in appropriate duty or retirement status, [or] correction of applicable records.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remedial options extend beyond back pay to administrative relief such as record correction, placement in retirement status, or restoration. See 28 U.S.C. § 1491(a)(2). Practitioners should plead and support equitable remedies as well as monetary claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on obtaining pay of a higher rank under the Military Pay Act
rubrics_metrics.description: The Military Pay Act generally cannot be used to obtain the salary of a higher rank for which the claimant was not selected; 'a service member is entitled only to the salary of the rank to which he [or she] is appointed and in which he [or she] serves.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two narrow exceptions permit recovery of higher-pay: (1) the plaintiff has satisfied all legal requirements for promotion but the military refused to recognize status; or (2) the decision not to promote led to the service member’s compelled discharge. See Smith v. Sec’y of the Army and related authorities. Plead facts to fit one of these exceptions when seeking higher-grade pay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreting 'may' in military pay statutes for money-mandating analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory provisions that state an incentive pay or bonus 'may' be made are presumptively discretionary, not money-mandating; discretionary payments are not money-mandating for Tucker Act purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, long-standing history and usage can rebut the presumption of discretion—some 'may' statutes have been treated as money-mandating (United States v. Larionoff). Practitioners must analyze statutory history, administrative practice, and precedent to argue whether a 'may' provision is in fact money-mandating. Cases: Doe v. United States; Deggins; Adair; Larionoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerequisites and process for disability benefits (PEB, Medical Evaluation Board role)
rubrics_metrics.description: To receive compensation or retirement benefits for military disability, a service member must suffer a permanent disability manifesting itself during active service; a Physical Evaluation Board (PEB) determines fitness for duty and entitlement to disability retirement or separation once a Medical Evaluation Board finds the soldier does not meet retention standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disputes commonly center on whether the medical profile at separation should have triggered MEB/PEB review. Correction boards can act in the place of a PEB or refer claims to a PEB; but where no PEB convened, board review (or its denial) controls accrual. Cases: Chambers; McHenry; Barnick; Sawyer. Litigators should develop the administrative medical record and show whether the PEB/MEB process was followed or improperly omitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporary Disability Retired List (TDRL) and separation vs retirement thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: If a service member’s condition is not 'of a permanent nature and stable,' the service may put the member on the Temporary Disability Retired List; a disability rating of less than 30% under the standard schedule of rating disabilities entitles the service member to a separation payment rather than a disability retirement benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand and plead the permanency/stability facts and the percentage rating rules; placement on TDRL or classification under <30% affects remedy (separation payment vs retirement). Cite 10 U.S.C. § 1201–1203 and relevant case law (Peoples, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Veterans Affairs Schedule for Rating Disabilities (VASRD) by the services
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory revision requires the Secretary to 'utilize the schedule for rating disabilities in use by the Department of Veterans Affairs (VASRD)' to the extent feasible when making disability determinations for purposes of the military disability statutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Though services apply the same VASRD, the purposes differ: the military uses it to determine fitness for duties of office/grade/rank, whereas the VA uses it post-discharge to evaluate civilian functional capacity. Expect differing outcomes even with the same schedule; rely on regulations and service-specific instructions (AFI, AR, SECNAVINST) and case law explaining the distinctions (Sabree quoting Haskins).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accrual and statute-of-limitations rule for disability retirement pay claims (board-triggered accrual)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disability retirement pay claims 'do not accrue until the appropriate [military] board either finally denies such a claim or refuses to hear it'; the decision by the first statutorily authorized board that hears or refuses to hear the claim is the triggering event for the six-year limitations period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A limited exception: if the service member had actual or constructive notice of the disability (and entitlement) at discharge, failing to request a hearing before discharge has the same effect as a refusal to provide board review and thereby triggers accrual. Courts assess whether the veteran's knowledge at discharge was sufficient to constitute waiver (Real; Chambers; Jan’s Helicopter cited elsewhere). Carefully develop facts on notice/knowledge and administrative opportunity for board review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit on courts considering de novo evidence; remand when record incomplete
rubrics_metrics.description: Following Florida Power & Light Co. v. Lorion, a lower court reviewing an agency action should generally remand to the agency to consider new evidence if the record before the court is incomplete; the Federal Circuit requires remand to a board to consider relevant evidence omitted in the first instance rather than allowing the court to consider new evidence in a supplemented record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts now typically limit review to the administrative record and will remand to military boards where a claim was not adequately addressed. Rare exceptions exist but are limited. Cases: Florida Power & Light Co.; Walls; Riser; Hale. Practitioners should develop the administrative record before filing suit and seek remand where relevant evidence was omitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Waiver/exhaustion consequences under Metz for claims presented to a correction board
rubrics_metrics.description: Metz holds that a plaintiff who brings a claim in court after a decision by a military board waives the claims or arguments he or she did not raise in initial or reconsideration petitions before the board; Metz effectively imposes a categorical exhaustion requirement on a military pay claimant who first seeks relief from a corrections board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claimant intends to litigate specific claims in court, they should ensure those claims are raised before the board (or file in Court of Federal Claims first, as discussed). Metz departs from earlier permissive approaches that allowed new de novo evidence in court—practitioners must plan administrative pleadings accordingly. Cite Metz v. United States.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circuit split on exhaustion and recognized exceptions (Ninth Circuit four-part test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some circuits require exhaustion of intramilitary administrative remedies for APA cases; the Ninth Circuit treats exhaustion as prudential and recognizes four circumstances in which exhaustion is not required: (1) intraservice remedies do not provide an opportunity for adequate relief; (2) petitioner will suffer irreparable harm if compelled to seek administrative relief; (3) administrative appeal would be futile; or (4) substantial constitutional questions are raised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must account for circuit-specific doctrine: D.C. Circuit and others favor exhaustion; Ninth (and some others) apply the four-part exception test (Wenger v. Monroe, Muhammad, etc.). Where district court jurisdiction is sought under the APA, consider whether exceptions apply or whether courts will stay proceedings pending board action (Montgomery; Nelson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissive option to file directly in Court of Federal Claims (Tucker Act suits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Military boards have been regarded as a 'permissive administrative remedy ... not a mandatory prerequisite to filing a Tucker Act suit challenging the discharge.' A plaintiff may opt to file suit directly in the Court of Federal Claims instead of seeking relief first before a military correction board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing in the Court of Federal Claims preserves the option of full evidentiary review and avoids potential waiver under Metz; Martinez explains benefits (avoiding staleness, loss of evidence, and allowing immediate judicial remedy). A claimant can file suit and request a stay to preserve both judicial remedy and right to board review. Plan strategy based on desired forum and exhaustion consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of correction boards for adversarial/fact-intensive claims (nonadversarial structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Correction boards were conceived as nonadversarial, investigatory bodies and may not be well-suited to collect or evaluate all evidence or to conduct trial-style factfinding (no direct testimony, cross-examination, or credibility assessments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certain claims—e.g., ineffective assistance of counsel—may be problematic before boards because of ex parte communications, withheld materials, and a paper-record posture (Helferty example). Practitioners should evaluate whether the claim requires adversarial fact-finding (favoring federal court) or can be adequately addressed administratively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ex parte communications and procedural fairness issues before correction boards
rubrics_metrics.description: Statute generally prohibits ex parte communications to boards (10 U.S.C. § 1556), though exceptions exist (classified information, legally prohibited releases); withholding of material at the board level can create due process concerns and lead to remand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inadequate disclosure to claimants or reliance on ex parte advisory opinions (even if withheld for privacy/classification reasons) can undermine the adequacy of board proceedings and support judicial intervention or remand. Cite Helferty and statutory provision 10 U.S.C. § 1556. Preserve discovery of what the board considered where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class-action practice in military pay/disability suits (Court of Federal Claims opt-in regime)
rubrics_metrics.description: A few suits have been certified as class actions under Rule 23 of the Rules of the Court of Federal Claims; the court allows only opt-in class actions (opt-out not permitted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In class actions like Sabo (PTSD class), courts closely supervise notice (direct mail to thousands, websites), delineation of claims, appointment of class counsel, and settlement terms. Settlement structuring considered categories of claimants (board decision status, severance vs retirement, TDRL placement, VA rating). Attorneys' fees often handled separately and may not be paid out of claimant settlement proceeds. Carefully design notice and opt-in procedures consistent with court rules and precedents (Sabo).

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedial approaches in reverse-discrimination class actions (remand vs lump-sum settlements)
rubrics_metrics.description: In reverse-discrimination actions, the government often urges remand for 'harmless error' analysis by reconstituted service boards to cure discriminatory criteria; the Federal Circuit adopted this remedial approach in Christian, but parties have sometimes settled with standard lump-sum payments to class members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remedies may include remand for harmless-error reevaluation or negotiated lump-sum payments and selective reprocessing (some plaintiffs may be given retention/back-pay). Settlement terms may include limited attorneys' fee percentages. Counsel should evaluate whether equitable reprocessing or settlement better serves clients given remedial limits and practicality.
